concepts: inosine short-chain fatty acids LC-MS/MS GC-MS quantification protocol human serum tumor microenvironment reference range

Are there established standardized measurement protocols or consensus guidelines for absolute quantification of inosine and short-chain fatty acids in human cancer patient serum or tumor tissue samples?
need.question: What standardized analytical protocols (LC-MS/MS or GC-MS parameters, sample processing standards) exist for quantifying absolute physiological concentrations of inosine and short-chain fatty acids in human serum or tumor tissue, and are there cancer-specific reference ranges or consensus statements?

usable_content: This study provides specific LC-MS/MS analytical parameters for quantifying adenosine and inosine in murine tumor tissues, including column type (ZORBAX RRHD Eclipse Plus C18), mobile phase gradients (water/acetonitrile with 0.1% FA), flow rate (300 µL min⁻¹), and MRM transitions (inosine 269.1/136.8, adenosine 268.1/135.9). It also describes a solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technique for measuring free metabolite concentrations in the tumor microenvironment using HLB-PAN fibers and kinetic calibration. A baseline adenosine concentration of 0.04 µM is reported for control mouse tumors. This study provides a detailed methodological framework for serum metabolite quantification using gas-chromatography/mass-spectrometry (GC/MS), which offers supporting technical parameters for the requested gap. The authors specify sample processing standards including serum separation (3,000 x g, 10 min, 4°C), storage conditions (−80°C), and extraction protocols (MeOH:H2O:CHCl3 = 2.5:1:1 with 2-isopropylmalic acid internal standard). The study outlines specific GC/MS instrument parameters such as column type (CP-SIL 8 CB), temperature programming (80°C to 330°C), and ion-source settings (200°C), along with quality control measures like calculating relative standard deviation (RSD%) and evaluating intra-day/inter-day variance. While the specific metabolites quantified (2-hydroxybutyrate, aspartic acid, kynurenine, cystamine) do not match the gap's target (inosine or short-chain fatty acids), the documented workflow serves as a reference template for establishing absolute physiological concentration protocols in human serum. The authors also demonstrate how to establish reference concentration ranges and cut-off values for cancer patients versus healthy controls using logistic regression and ROC analysis, providing a statistical model for defining cancer-specific reference ranges even though the specific analytes differ.
